text: God wasn't in the wind, the earthquake or the fire. Only the still small voice drew Elijah out of his cave.
explanation:
At Mount Horeb, where the law was given, a great wind tore at the mountains, then came an earthquake, then fire. Those had been the marks of Elijah's own ministry: drought, storm, fire from heaven. "But the Lord was not in the wind… not in the earthquake… not in the fire." Through all of it, Elijah stayed hidden in the cave.

Then came "a still small voice," and "when Elijah heard it, he wrapped his face in his mantle and went out." Just as Adam hid among the trees, punishment only drives people into hiding. Only the gentle voice of grace draws a sinner out to stand before God. "The goodness of God leads you to repentance."

text: When James and John wanted to call down fire like Elijah, Jesus rebuked them, not the Samaritans who'd rejected Him.
explanation:
A Samaritan village refused to welcome Jesus. James and John asked, "Lord, do You want us to command fire to come down from heaven and consume them, just as Elijah did?" It seemed like a biblical idea: Elijah had done it. "But He turned and rebuked them, and said, 'You do not know what manner of spirit you are of. For the Son of Man did not come to destroy men's lives but to save them.'"

Then they simply went to another village. Some believers still think a real prophet must thunder judgment. But Jesus said that spirit isn't His. Under grace, we're sent not to call down fire, but to bring life.

text: New Testament prophecy builds up, draws near and comforts. Text someone an encouraging word today.
explanation:
"He who prophesies speaks edification and exhortation and comfort to men." Exhortation means calling someone near. In the Old Testament, most prophets carried a ministry of condemnation, and God sent them to. But Jesus said, "All the prophets and the law prophesied until John." The last minister of condemnation was John the Baptist, whose name means "God is gracious."

Every believer can speak on God's behalf this way. When someone comes to mind, send them a message: "I sense favour coming your way. Something good is about to happen." You never know how badly they needed to hear it. "Exhort one another daily."

text: "If he makes them void after he has heard them, then he shall bear her guilt." Jesus bore the guilt of our vow to keep the law.
explanation:
Under the law, if a wife made a binding vow and her husband heard it and said nothing, the vow stood. If he cancelled it later, "then he shall bear her guilt." It reads like an old regulation about vows, but it hides a picture of Christ.

At Sinai, before God had spoken a single commandment, Israel vowed, "All that the Lord has spoken we will do." It was the presumption of people who didn't yet know their own weakness, and the golden calf soon followed. The Lord let that vow stand for centuries. Then our Husband came to cancel it, and to do so, He had to bear our guilt Himself. That's why we're no longer under the law.

text: Jesus could have been stoned, the law's usual execution. He was hung on a tree, because "cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree."
explanation:
Stoning was the death penalty the law prescribed. Crucifixion was a foreign, Roman cruelty. Jesus could have borne our sins and died by stoning, but God had a further purpose: "Christ has redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us (for it is written, 'Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree')."

The law's curse is spelled out in Deuteronomy 28: sickness, poverty, broken homes, early death. And it falls on anyone who fails to keep everything, not on those who merely do their best. By hanging on a tree, Jesus absorbed that curse so you could be lifted out from under the law entirely, and righteously so.

text: People fled from Moses' shining face. They ran toward Jesus when He came down the mountain.
explanation:
When Moses came down from Sinai with the law, his face shone, and the people were afraid to come near. At the foot of the mountain, the law could only judge: the golden calf was destroyed, and the sinners with it. When Jesus came down from the Mount of Transfiguration, "all the people… were greatly amazed, and running to Him, greeted Him."

At the foot of His mountain was a boy tormented by a demon. Jesus cast out the spirit and gave the boy back to his father. The law destroys the sinner along with the sin; grace separates the person from the bondage and saves them. Every ray from His unveiled face says: your sins are gone.

text: God sent Elijah to a widow in Sidon, the hometown of Jezebel herself. Where sin abounds, grace abounds much more.
explanation:
Jezebel, the queen who led Israel into Baal worship, was a princess of Sidon. Yet when Elijah needed food during the famine, God sent him to "Zarephath, which belongs to Sidon," to a Gentile widow. There, "the bin of flour was not used up, nor did the jar of oil run dry."

When Jesus pointed this out in Nazareth ("many widows were in Israel… but to none of them was Elijah sent except to Zarephath, in the region of Sidon"), the crowd was furious. They couldn't stand grace that reached past them to the very heartland of their enemy. But that's how far God's grace reaches, even to you.
